title: Arcadia Bio POC scoping - open-model shortlist
summary: POC scoping for an extraction-and-summarization workflow in the biomedical domain. Discussed success criteria (latency, extraction F1, throughput), workload sizing, benchmark plan, timelines, and open-model shortlist with quality/latency tradeoffs and multilingual needs.
topics: Model shortlist: Llama-2 variants, Mistral, Llama-3, Bio-specific LLMs

transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jesse Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML - Arcadia Bio), Tom Reynolds (CTO - Arcadia Bio), Priya Nair (PM - Arcadia)

[00:00] Jesse Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a quick intro. I'm Jesse, I'm the AE working with Arcadia, and Maya is our solutions engineer. we have about 45 minutes — high level scoping for the POC right?
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: yep thanks. wanted to focus on two things: accuracy for entity extraction and clean summarization for clinicians, and also throughput — we have to process batches overnight, but we also want sub-second latency for the realtime UI.
[00:25] Tom Reynolds: and security questions up front — SOC 2, K M S integration, and audit logs, we need to know where data lives.
[00:32] Maya Singh: totally. we'll cover the security doc links after. for the POC we usually run a 2-3 week bench with 1k to 5k representative records, measure F1/precision/recall for extraction and ROUGE/BLEU-ish metrics for summary quality, plus p99 latencies and tokens/sec throughput.
[00:48] Priya Nair: ideal timeline for us is a decision by end of March. we can get samples to you next week. what's the typical model shortlist for biomedical-ish workloads when you prefer open models?
[01:02] Jesse Park: good question. common approach is 1) a strong open-weight model like Llama-3 or Llama-2-Chat-70B, 2) a lighter Mistral or Llama-2-13B variant for latency/cost balance, and 3) a domain-adapted small bio model if available — e.g., BioMed LLM or a fine-tuned Llama-2-13B. we also include a quantized path, like 4-bit int8 quant, to test cost/latency tradeoffs.
[01:27] Lena Ortiz: we care about multilingual — Spanish and Portuguese notes — and domain terms are dense. will off-the-shelf Llama-3 handle that?
[01:34] Maya Singh: Llama-3 has strong multilingual capability, but domain-specific jargon can still need fine-tuning or prompt engineering. the benchmark should include multilingual slices. also, we'll test prefix caching for repeated prompts — that can reduce tokens and latency.
[01:48] Tom Reynolds: about throughput — our overnight batch is ~200k notes/day, average 350 tokens each, peak concurrent UI traffic maybe 30 qps. what's reasonable?
[01:57] Jesse Park: for 30 qps interactive, you'd want a smaller model or dedicated capacity; Redwood Dedicate — sorry Redwood Dedicated — with pinned GPUs helps guarantee p99 latency. for batch of 200k, batching + async workers on hosted will be cost-effective. Maya, any ballpark numbers?
[02:12] Maya Singh: ballpark: Llama-3-70B on a single A100-ish device does ~5-10 tokens/sec in real inference without optimizations for long sequences; but with batching and quantization we can hit 30-50 tokens/sec for 8-bit paths. for the interactive 30 qps you'd likely run multiple replicas or a dedicated pool. for Llama-2-13B or Mistral, latency per request drops a lot — p50 under 200ms if you tune batching.
[02:36] Lena Ortiz: our success criteria — quick draft: extraction F1 >= 0.88, summary acceptance >= 85% by clinicians, p99 latency < 800ms for interactive, and cost under $X per 1k notes (we'll define X later). does that map to a POC you can run?
[02:49] Jesse Park: yes that's reasonable. we'll operationalize that into the bench config. two notes: 1) p99 at <800ms depends on model size and whether it's dedicated, 2) quality thresholds mean we may need light fine-tuning. fine-tuning adds time but short few-shot evals can help scope.
[03:05] Priya Nair: fine-tuning timeline? we have some annotated data but not huge volumes.
[03:10] Maya Singh: few-shot or instruction-tuning with a few hundred examples often moves the needle. full fine-tune or LoRA might take additional setup and review, but we can start with prompt engineering and a 100-200 annotated examples during the bench to see if that's enough.
[03:22] Tom Reynolds: security again quickly — KMS for customer-managed keys, SSO/SAML, and audit trail. how mature are those in Redwood Private?
[03:30] Jesse Park: Redwood Private supports KMS integration and on-prem options; we have SOC 2 Type II and per-route audit logs. I'll share the security pack after the call. for the hosted test, we can enable retention policies and disable persistent logs for the POC.
[03:42] Lena Ortiz: ok thanks.
[03:45] Maya Singh: going back to model shortlist — we usually test three axes: quality, latency/cost, domain-adaptation. Suggested shortlist for Arcadia: 1) Llama-3-70B (quality anchor), 2) Mistral-Instruct-22B (cost/latency balance), 3) Llama-2-13B fine-tuned/LoRA on your notes (domain). optionally include a Bio-specific smaller model if you want to test domain pretraining.
[04:08] Jesse Park: also include Llama-3-70B in an 8-bit quant path to get a realistic cost comparison.
[04:13] Priya Nair: what's the expected cost delta between hosted and Dedicated?
[04:17] Maya Singh: hosted is pay-as-you-go; Dedicated is reserved capacity — you trade a commit for predictable perf and lower per-token cost at scale. for a POC with 1k-5k samples, hosted is easiest. Dedicated makes sense when you're hitting sustained traffic or need isolation. we'll provide cost comparatives in the model shortlist doc.
[04:33] Lena Ortiz: benchmark design — we want slices: clinical notes short (<200 tokens), long (>1000 tokens), Spanish, Portuguese, and specialty terms. also blind labeling by clinicians for summary acceptance. can Redwood run the whole bench or do you need us to host samples?
[04:46] Maya Singh: we can run it on Redwood hosted nodes with your sample dataset securely uploaded to a presigned S3. we'll run the 3-model comparison, and produce metrics: extraction F1, precision/recall, summary ROUGE/clinician acceptance, p50/p90/p99 latencies, cost per 1k notes.
[04:59] Tom Reynolds: about data residency — some notes must not leave EU. is regional hosting available?
[05:04] Jesse Park: yes, we have EU region hosting and Private deployments if you need on-prem. for the POC we can route EU data to EU region. I'll annotate that in the security doc.
[05:13] Lena Ortiz: any model licensing issues with Llama-3?
[05:16] Jesse Park: Llama-3 is open but check your legal; we provide vetted performance profiles and can recommend vetted weights. we also include a note on model cards and license considerations in the follow-up.
[05:25] Priya Nair: can we get a quick matrix that shows for each model: expected p99 latency (hosted), tokens/sec, estimated cost per 1k notes, and expected qualitative fit for biomedical?
[05:34] Maya Singh: yes that's exactly what we'll send. we'll include the quantized path for each model.
[05:38] Lena Ortiz: one more: evaluation tooling — can Redwood run clinician blind reviews in the console or do we need external tools?
[05:46] Maya Singh: Redwood Console has exportable CSVs and hooks to integrate with your review workflow; we can also set up a small dashboard with sample outputs for clinicians to mark accept/reject.
[05:55] Jesse Park: ok quick recap and next steps — Jesse to send model shortlist + cost and security pack; Arcadia to share 1k sample records and labeling schema; Maya to run benchmark across 3 models and return CSV of metrics; schedule follow-up week of Mar 16.
[06:09] Priya Nair: timeline sounds good.
[06:12] Tom Reynolds: a practical note — if we see that Llama-3 meets accuracy but cost is too high, what's the path? quantization and L2-13B fine-tune?
[06:21] Maya Singh: yep typical path is 1) quantize 70B or run it in lower-precision inference for spot checks, 2) shift interactive workload to 13-22B variants with a fine-tune/LoRA to regain domain performance, 3) if needed move to Dedicated to reduce latency and predictable cost.
[06:36] Lena Ortiz: are there pitfalls you've seen in POCs with clinical text?
[06:39] Maya Singh: common: tokenization splitting biomedical tokens oddly; hallucination on rare drugs; and long-context truncation causing missed entities. we mitigate with prompt templates, entity-aware prompts, and long-context kernels. also check how KV cache is handled — sometimes transcrip — sorry transcription errors earlier but the point is caching helps interactive performance.
[06:58] Jesse Park: perfect. i'll also include a checklist: data upload, redacted samples, consent confirmation, and contact for legal review.
[07:06] Priya Nair: ok thanks everyone. last question — sample size for quick signal: is 1k enough?
[07:11] Maya Singh: 1k gives a quick signal; 3k+ is better for statistical stability across slices. for clinical acceptance testing, plan for couple hundred labeled summaries for clinician review.
[07:24] Tom Reynolds: sounds good. thanks.
[07:27] Jesse Park: thanks all, i'll follow up with the doc and we can reconvene after benchmarks.

[End of transcript]
